stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation has a new prescription for edoxaban. The calculated creatinine clearance is 108 mL/min. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Administer edoxaban as prescribed because higher creatinine clearance improves its stroke-prevention efficacy
options.B: Question the prescription because current U.S. labeling states edoxaban should not be used for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation when CrCl is greater than 95 mL/min
options.C: Reduce the edoxaban dose by half because every CrCl above 95 mL/min requires dose reduction rather than a different anticoagulant
options.D: Hold all anticoagulation permanently because a high CrCl is a contraindication to anticoagulant therapy in general

rationale: Edoxaban has a boxed limitation for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: it should not be used when creatinine clearance exceeds 95 mL/min because efficacy for prevention of ischemic stroke was reduced compared with warfarin in this group. Renal function therefore must be assessed before initiation. This restriction is specific to edoxaban use for NVAF and does not mean anticoagulation itself is contraindicated.
educational_objective: Identify the edoxaban NVAF limitation in clients with CrCl greater than 95 mL/min and question an unsafe prescription.
source_version_date: DailyMed updated July 10, 2025; labeling revised October 2023
source_locator: Boxed Warning; Sections 1.1, 2.1 and 5.1 — do not use for NVAF when CrCl >95 mL/min because of increased ischemic stroke risk versus warfarin
source_claim_supported: For NVAF, edoxaban should not be used when CrCl exceeds 95 mL/min; renal function must be assessed before therapy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication safety, contraindications and monitoring
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — edoxaban renal-function limitation
correction_summary: Replaced indication recall with an explicit boxed-warning safety decision and limited the claim to nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, avoiding inappropriate generalization to DVT/PE treatment.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Current DailyMed boxed warning and NVAF dosing sections verified.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: CrCl >95 restriction is specific and explicit for NVAF.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect; high CrCl is associated with reduced efficacy in NVAF.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; label says do not use, not halve dose.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; alternative anticoagulation may be appropriate.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches the boxed warning.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Checked indication specificity, Cockcroft-Gault requirement and DVT/PE differences; no unresolved conflict.
